conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived, not to judge or label you in any way. We’ll use a quick, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past week, and it helps us spot anything that might benefit from extra support. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about “right” answers. Ready to start?

In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much at all. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute baby video or if my husband makes a joke, but it feels forced—like I’m doing it because I know I’m supposed to, not because it feels funny inside. Most of the time I’m just too tired or tense to find anything amusing.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

No… not really. Maybe once or twice when my husband pulled a silly face at the baby I cracked a little smile, but it disappeared fast. Laughing feels kind of impossible most of the time—like I’m too heavy inside to get there.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not very often. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels kind of… flat. Once in a while I’ll think, “Maybe it would be nice to go out,” but the feeling fades before I actually want to do it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle or I can’t figure out what he needs, my head jumps straight to “I’m a bad mom.” I know it’s probably not fair, but I keep thinking I should be handling everything better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. Even when everything looks fine—he’s breathing, he’s fed, he’s sleeping—I’ll suddenly feel this wave of “what if something happens?” The thoughts just loop: Is he too hot? Too cold? What if he spits up and chokes? I’ll check the monitor a dozen times, and still my chest feels tight. I know it’s not rational, but I can’t shut it off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few times this week. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air. Nothing’s happening—baby’s asleep, the house is quiet—but suddenly I’m sure something awful is about to go wrong. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like the dishes, the laundry, the feedings, the pumping, the texts I haven’t answered—they all pile up and I feel I can’t catch my breath. Some mornings I just stare at the mess and want to crawl back under the blanket, but I get up anyway because the baby needs me. I manage, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t settle—kept replaying everything I might have done wrong or imagining scary “what-ifs” about the baby. Most nights this week it took me over an hour to fall asleep, and when I do drift off I wake up again with my heart pounding, sure I heard him cry (even when he hasn’t).
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… pretty much every day. It’s not crying-all-day sad, just this heavy, gray feeling that follows me around. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel like I’m drowning in it. Some afternoons I just sit there staring out the window feeling empty, even when nothing “bad” has happened.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week. Once was when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing him; the other time was after a shower—just saw my reflection, felt huge and unfamiliar, and the tears started. Both times I tried to keep it quiet so my husband wouldn’t worry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s crossed my mind a couple of times, mostly at night when I can’t settle. It’s never a plan or anything—just this quick, scary flash of “what if I weren’t here.” I shove it away right after, but it’s shaken me that the thought even shows up.

Hearing how hard things feel right now, I'm struck by how much you're managing while carrying this heavy, gray mood every day. You describe smiling only because you know you're supposed to, feeling like you're <quote>failing him</quote> when the baby won't settle, and being haunted by sudden <sym>panic</sym> and <sym>what-ifs</sym> that keep you checking the monitor over and over. Yet you still get up because your baby needs you, which shows real strength even if it feels like <quote>treading water</quote>.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports virtually no ability to laugh or find humor, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports marked reduction in enjoyment and anticipation, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame ('I do that a lot') tied to motherhood tasks, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive, uncontrollable worry occurring daily despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden panic episodes multiple times in the past week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response shows frequent daily overwhelm yet some functional coping, aligning with "sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleep disruption, racing thoughts, and anxiety preventing both falling and staying asleep.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily sadness ('pretty much every day') with persistent, heavy, empty feelings that intrude during routine tasks, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurrent intrusive self-harm thoughts, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 24 (≥14) places you in the <med>high-risk</med> range. Items map to core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: persistent <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day (Q8=3), markedly diminished interest or pleasure (Q1=3,Q2=2), inappropriate guilt (Q3=3), <sym>insomnia</sym> (Q7=3), fatigue/loss of energy (Q6=2), psychomotor agitation via <sym>panic</sym> episodes (Q5=2), and recurrent <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> (Q10=2). The combination meets screening threshold for urgent evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health team for full assessment and safety planning
2. Call your local 24/7 crisis line or 988 if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and whether an <med>SSRI</med> compatible with breastfeeding might help
4. Enlist your partner or a trusted adult to take over one night feeding so you can get a 4-5-hour stretch of uninterrupted sleep
5. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress after interventions start
6. Share these results with your baby's pediatrician so the whole care team can coordinate support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: self-report on 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire, 2 wks postpartum

Symptoms endorsed (frequency/severity):
- Anhedonia (marked loss of laughter/pleasure)
- Persistent low mood, described as “heavy, gray,” daily
- Daily excessive guilt/self-blame (“bad mom” cognitions)
- Anxious and panic-type episodes (heart racing, air-hunger) most days; intrusive “what-if” thoughts about infant safety
- Overwhelm and sense of “treading water” with routine tasks
- Initial and middle insomnia linked to racing thoughts
- Two crying spells this week
- Passive suicidal ideation (“what if I weren’t here”) at night, no plan or intent

Pattern: symptoms present most days, interfere with functioning and attachment experiences.

Risk flags:
- Passive self-harm thoughts → safety concern
- Anxiety and panic symptoms meet clinical threshold for further assessment
- Sleep disruption compounds mood liability

Screening impression: High likelihood of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; rule-out postpartum anxiety disorder; urgent safety evaluation indicated.

Next step: Recommend immediate comprehensive mental-health assessment (including safety plan) and consideration of expedited referral to perinatal psychiatry.
